Explain in your own words what 'Differentiation, Dedifferentiation and Redifferentiation; Development' refers to.
questions.a: Cells derived from meristems undergo differentiation into specialised cells, dedifferentiation regains division capacity forming interfascicular cambium, and redifferentiation matures them again; development of the plant also shows plasticity such as heterophylly and is followed by senescence and death.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Differentiation, Dedifferentiation and Redifferentiation; Development'.
questions.a: Heterophylly in cotton and coriander shows plasticity, where leaves of juvenile and mature plants take different shapes in response to environment or phases of life.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Differentiation, Dedifferentiation and Redifferentiation; Development' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 13.2 Differentiation, Dedifferentiation, Redifferentiation, 13.3 Development (source: kebo113.txt sections 13.2, 13.3)

concepts.title: Plant Growth Regulators: Auxins, Gibberellins, Cytokinins, Ethylene and ABA

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Plant Growth Regulators: Auxins, Gibberellins, Cytokinins, Ethylene and ABA' refers to.
questions.a: Plant growth regulators include auxins promoting apical dominance and rooting, gibberellins causing bolting and internode elongation, cytokinins promoting cell division and delaying senescence, gaseous ethylene promoting fruit ripening and triple response, and abscisic acid as the stress hormone closing stomata.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Plant Growth Regulators: Auxins, Gibberellins, Cytokinins, Ethylene and ABA'.
questions.a: Auxin's apical dominance and cytokinin's promotion of lateral buds act in opposition, and ethylene is unique among PGRs in being a gas that hastens ripening.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Plant Growth Regulators: Auxins, Gibberellins, Cytokinins, Ethylene and ABA' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Photoperiodism and Vernalisation' refers to.
questions.a: Photoperiodism is the response of plants to the relative length of light and dark periods, classifying them into long day, short day and day neutral plants, while vernalisation is the induction of flowering by prolonged cold treatment as in winter varieties of wheat and barley.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Photoperiodism and Vernalisation'.
questions.a: The site of photoperiodic perception is the leaf, and vernalisation prevents precocious reproductive development late in the season, with the hormone behind it named vernalin.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Photoperiodism and Vernalisation' taught, and from which source text?
